with a wide range of applications. The field has seen rapid advancements, driven by the need to optimize the trade-off between detection accuracy and computational efficiency. Among existing models, the YOLO family has emerged as a leading solution, offering a well-balanced performance that makes it particularly suitable for real-time applications on embedded systems.As detection tasks become more complex, choosing the right model for a given task becomes increasingly important. While newer architectures may show improved performance on standard benchmarks, older models can still outperform them in specialized scenarios. This highlights the necessity for efficient model selection tailored to specific task requirements.Neural Architecture Search (NAS) provides a promising approach to this problem by automating model design. However, the effectiveness of NAS largely depends on the quality and flexibility of the search space. In this paper, we propose a novel NAS technique that explores the search space in a hybrid manner combining both block-level and operation-level searches. Specifically, we introduce modular blocks as new search units and leverage components from YOLOv3 to YOLOv11 to construct a rich and diverse search space.Our method enables task-specific optimization by reusing proven modular blocks and operations, achieving an effective balance between speed and accuracy. We validate MBNAS on COCO and VisDrone datasets and demonstrate high-performing models optimized for deployment on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier board using Communications Applications Conference (SIU)"],"is-referenced-by-count":2,"URL":"https://doi.org/10.1109/siu66497.2025.11112171","type":"proceedings-article"},{"abstract":"<jats:p>Hyperspectral image classification (HSIC) is a crucial task for remote sensing applications, requiring accurate pixel-level labeling while effectively capturing both spectral and spatial information. Traditional convolutional neural network architectures often struggle to balance local texture detail and global contextual consistency, and existing neural architecture search (NAS) methods rarely incorporate attention mechanisms, limiting their performance. To address these challenges, this study proposes a multi-scale Transformer-based NAS framework (TR-NAS) for fine-grained hyperspectral image classification. The framework combines local cube sampling, shallow and deep multi-scale convolutions, and a searchable Transformer module that adaptively selects global, local window, and multi-scale attention operators. Lightweight enhanced convolution operators, including dual-gated (DG-Conv) and mixed depthwise (MixConv) convolutions, are incorporated to improve spectral discrimination and scale robustness. Extensive experiments on the PU and Hanchuan datasets demonstrate that TR-NAS achieves superior classification accuracy, stability, and boundary consistency compared to traditional methods and existing NAS architectures, showing improved robustness to spectral similarity and spatial heterogeneity in complex remote sensing scenes.</jats:p>","DOI":"10.3390/rs18101586","type":"journal-article","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["Multi-Scale Transformer-Based Neural Architecture Search for Hyperspectral Image Classification"],"author":[{"ORCID":"https://orcid.org/0000-0002-9118-230X","authenticated-orcid":false,"given":"Aili","family":"Wang","sequence":"first","affiliation":[{"name":"Heilongjiang Province Key Laboratory of Laser Spectroscopy Technology and Application, Harbin University of Science and Technology, Harbin 150080, China"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Xinyu","family":"Liu","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[{"name":"Heilongjiang Province Key Laboratory of Laser Spectroscopy Technology and Application, Harbin University of Science and Technology, Harbin 150080, China"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"given":"Haisong","family":"Chen","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[{"name":"School of Integrated Circuit, Shenzhen Polytechnic University, Shenzhen 518115, China"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"container-title":["Remote Sensing"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026,5,15]]},"URL":"https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18101586"},{"abstract":"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    3D medical image classification is crucial for improving diagnostic accuracy and treatment planning, but it encounters challenges due to the complexity and variability of volumetric data. While 3D Convolutional Neural Networks offer potential solutions, designing effective architectures is complex and resource-intensive. Neural Architecture Search automates this process, optimizing network designs for specific tasks, thereby improving model performance. This study introduces a novel extension of the PBC-NAS method for 3D medical image classification, aiming to balance prediction accuracy and model complexity. We focus on optimizing neural network architectures using Neural Architecture Search for six different 3D datasets from MedMNIST3D, including OrganMNIST3D, NoduleMNIST3D, FractureMNIST3D, AdrenalMNIST3D, VesselMNIST3D, and SynapseMNIST3D, which are derived from real-world clinical imaging datasets. We have compared our method with state-of-the-art handcrafted networks, AutoML frameworks and recent NAS studies in terms of prediction performance and model complexity. The proposed NAS methods demonstrate superior performance compared to state-of-the-art handcrafted networks and AutoML frameworks. Our proposed model (Ours #3
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$^\dagger$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ) achieves the highest average Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.915 and accuracy (ACC) of 0.847 (best result across three independent runs), outperforming all handcrafted networks and AutoML frameworks. Compared to other NAS-based methods, all proposed models achieve higher average AUC scores, and it is important to note that they do not rely on data augmentation, pre-processing, or feature selection, unlike the competing NAS methods which do use data augmentation during training. The study also highlights significant reductions in computational complexity, with FLOPs reduced by up to 45.51 times and parameters by up to 211 times compared to ResNet models. An ablation study reveals that while fine-tuning a model optimized for one dataset can achieve competitive results on other datasets, dataset-specific NAS is crucial for optimal performance. Despite this, the ablation results still outperform ResNets and AutoML frameworks in terms of average AUC and ACC. The study concludes that the proposed NAS approach effectively optimizes neural network architectures for complex 3D medical image classification tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance without data augmentation.
